headings.title: Introduction to Wound Classification in Midwifery Practice
headings.content: A wound is simply a break in the integrity of the skin or mucous membranes. In midwifery practice, understanding wounds is crucial not just for surgical sites like episiotomies and Caesarean section incisions, but also for managing perineal tears that happen during vaginal delivery. Classifying wounds properly helps midwives choose the right care plan, predict healing times, and spot early signs of trouble like infection. Without a clear system to describe how a wound happened and how deep it goes, communication between healthcare workers breaks down, and patient safety suffers.

headings.title: Classification by Mechanism of Injury
headings.content:
Wounds are often grouped by how they were created. Knowing the mechanism helps predict how much tissue is damaged and how the body will try to repair it.

- **Incision**: A clean, straight cut caused by a sharp instrument like a scalpel during a Caesarean section.
- **Laceration**: A jagged, irregular tear in the skin caused by blunt trauma or excessive stretching, common during difficult vaginal deliveries.
- **Abrasion**: A superficial scrape where the top layer of skin is rubbed off, usually from friction.
- **Puncture**: A deep, narrow hole caused by a sharp, pointed object like a needle or thorn.

headings.title: Categorization by Depth and Tissue Loss
headings.content:
The depth of a wound determines how long healing will take and what layers of the body are involved. 

- **Superficial wounds** involve only the epidermis, the top layer of the skin. These usually heal quickly through simple regeneration without leaving a scar.
- **Partial-thickness wounds** extend through the epidermis and into the dermis. Skin structures like hair follicles and sweat glands may remain, helping the area re-epithelialize.
- **Full-thickness wounds** destroy the dermis and extend down into subcutaneous fat, muscle, or even bone. These require complex healing processes involving granulation tissue and scar formation.

headings.title: Clean, Contaminated, and Infected Wounds
headings.content:
Wounds are also classified by their degree of microbial contamination. This helps midwives anticipate infection risks and manage hygiene properly.

- **Clean wounds** are uninfected operative wounds where no inflammation is met and the respiratory, alimentary, or genital tracts are not entered.
- **Contaminated wounds** include open, fresh, accidental wounds or surgical procedures with a major break in sterile technique. Bacteria are present, but active infection has not yet taken hold.
- **Infected wounds** show clear signs of active microbial multiplication, such as pus, foul odor, redness, localized heat, and severe pain.

headings.title: Common Obstetric and Gynecological Wounds
headings.content: Midwives frequently encounter specific types of wounds unique to maternal and reproductive health. An **episiotomy** is a surgical incision of the perineum made during second-stage labor to ease delivery. **Perineal tears** occur naturally when the baby's head stretches the vaginal opening beyond its tissue limit; these are graded from first-degree (involving only skin) to fourth-degree (extending into the rectal mucosa). **Caesarean section scars** are surgical abdominal wounds that require careful postoperative observation for dehiscence or hematoma formation.

headings.title: Clinical Implications for Patient Assessment
headings.content: Accurate wound assessment guides day-to-day clinical decisions in the ward. Midwives must evaluate wounds regularly using systematic parameters, often remembered by clinical acronyms or structured frameworks like size, depth, edge condition, exudate amount, and surrounding skin health. Failing to recognize a changing wound profile can lead to delayed healing or severe systemic sepsis. Documentation must be precise, recording any changes in pain levels or discharge characteristics so the entire healthcare team stays informed.
